statement: Peripheral GLP-1 receptor agonists do not substantially cross the intact blood-brain barrier; they reach brain targets via circumventricular organs, tanycytes, slow adsorptive transcytosis, and vagal/NTS relay.
note: Brain effect does not imply broad brain penetration — the central misconception this module exists to dissolve.

statement: Vagal afferents to the NTS carry a substantial portion of GLP-1's intake-suppressing signal; the relay is indirect and partial rather than the sole route.

Brain PPG-NTS neurons are a phasic satiation and aversive-interoceptive signal — recruited by large meals, gastric distension, and visceral stress, and suppressed by fasting — not a tonic appetite regulator.
note: Pharmacological agonists sustain chronically a system nature deploys phasically — the framing that interprets both intended effects and side-effect spectra.

statement: Arcuate and NTS circuits drive meal termination; the gut-brain satiety pathway is the standard-explainer surface and is visibly incomplete on its own.

GLP-1RA reduces motivational salience for high-energy palatable rewards — lower progressive-ratio breakpoints and reduced food-cue striatal activation. The defensible synthesis is rebalancing of incentive salience, not blunting.
Cue-evoked mesolimbic dopamine signalling is reduced under GLP-1RA — the canonical 'dopamine down' account of reduced wanting.
note: 'Dopamine down' is not permitted as a final explanation — see the contradicting photometry claim.

statement: In-vivo fibre photometry shows preserved or even enhanced consummatory VTA dopamine signals under semaglutide, alongside reduced cumulative consumption — directly complicating the simple blunting account.
note: The contradiction is the feature: it renders as graph structure on the wanting outcome, not as a buried caveat.

statement: The VTA expresses GLP-1R on a subset of TH+ dopamine neurons; local exendin-4 microinjection reduces palatable intake.
Multiple human randomised trials show GLP-1RA reduces alcohol consumption and craving — the strongest cross-reward evidence outside food.
Semaglutide's alcohol suppression involves central amygdala GABAergic modulation, not solely dopaminergic effects — the mechanism is not a dopamine monoculture.
Large EHR cohorts report roughly 85% lower recorded substance-use outcomes under GLP-1RA — implausibly large as pure pharmacology, and best presented as suggestive rather than definitive.
Acute central GLP-1 in the central amygdala is reliably anxiogenic without robust HPA engagement.
note: Rodent · central · acute — translation-fragile. Not the same as chronic peripheral therapy in humans.

statement: PVN GLP-1R drives HPA-axis activation (CRH, corticosterone) without anxiety-like behaviour — PVN and CeA dissociate on stress versus anxiety.
Chronic peripheral therapeutic dosing in humans appears neutral to mildly favourable on affect; population-level suicidality signals do not support a causal link and lean weakly protective.
The phase-3 EVOKE and EVOKE+ trials did not show benefit of oral semaglutide on cognitive decline in mild cognitive impairment / mild Alzheimer's disease.
note: The cautionary precedent: observational neurocognitive signals can fail to replicate in randomised trials.

statement: Rodent and cellular work shows BDNF increase, anti-inflammatory action, and hippocampal plasticity — encouraging preclinically, but not borne out in human trials.
note: Held in tension with EVOKE — the atlas does not present GLP-1RAs as cognition-protective in humans.

statement: A dorsolateral-septum to lateral-hypothalamus projection may contribute to GLP-1 appetite effects.
openQuestion: Does the septo-hypothalamic route carry an independent appetite signal?

statement: Top-down prefrontal modulation of reward valuation under GLP-1RA is plausible but currently speculative.
openQuestion: Is reduced cue reactivity driven by cortical reappraisal or by subcortical reweighting?

statement: The BNST sustains negative affect; a CeA-to-BNST projection is implicated in the aversive-affect branch of GLP-1 signalling.
PPG-NTS neurons are suppressed during negative energy balance; their quiescence lifts inhibition on food-seeking and appetitive behaviour, and ablation does not alter ad libitum intake.
note: The clearest evidence against a tonic-appetite-regulator reading of the central GLP-1 system.

statement: Vagal input to PPG-NTS neurons is not carried by GLP-1R-expressing afferents; peripheral GLP-1 does not principally engage PPG via the vagus — central and peripheral GLP-1 systems act largely independently.
Gastric distension drives a phasic burst of PPG-NTS activity; chemogenetic activation potently suppresses eating — the canonical secondary-satiation 'stop' signal.
Restraint stress and visceral malaise recruit PPG-NTS neurons strongly; ablating them blocks stress-induced hypophagia — the neurons do double duty as secondary satiation and aversive interoception.

GLP-1RA reduces nicotine reward: exendin-4 blunts nicotine-induced accumbal dopamine and conditioned place preference in rodents, and cigarettes per day fell in the smoker subgroup of a semaglutide alcohol trial. The human signal is secondary, not a dedicated smoking trial.
note: Tirzepatide is barely studied in this paradigm; the rodent work is acute experimental dosing.

statement: Liraglutide reduces heroin self-administration and drug-induced reinstatement in rats; human evidence is observational only — no opioid-use-disorder randomised trial has read out.
note: The EHR opioid signal carries the same implausibly large effect size and confounding-by-indication problem flagged across the cross-reward page.

statement: Exendin-4 reduces cocaine self-administration and reinstatement in mice. There is no human stimulant-use trial, and stimulant addiction is mechanistically less coupled to metabolic and satiety signalling than alcohol or food.
note: Preclinical only — to be read as a mechanistic hypothesis, not a clinical claim.

statement: Reduced gambling, compulsive shopping, and other non-consummatory behavioural rewards under GLP-1RAs are reported only as case reports and clinician anecdote — uncontrolled, and assuming rather than showing a shared incentive-salience mechanism.
openQuestion: Does incentive-salience down-weighting extend to non-consummatory behavioural rewards, or does the apparent signal reflect report bias?

statement: Amygdalar GLP-1R density is substantially higher in non-human primates than in rodents — so the rodent acute-anxiogenic findings may amplify rather than attenuate in humans, cutting against dismissing them as a pure rodent artefact.
openQuestion: Does denser primate amygdalar GLP-1R translate to larger human affective effects than rodent models predict?
